data.content_ref: inline:The claim asserts the Popperian 'leap of faith' is 'grounded solely in the logical asymmetry of falsification.' This is internally inconsistent with the target's own mechanism, which does not derive the preference from the asymmetry at all but from three additional substantive methodological commitments: (1) that corroboration 'identifies the theory that has withstood the most severe attempts at falsification,' (2) that this makes it 'the most testable and thus the most informative candidate for further criticism,' and (3) that 'choosing it is a methodological rule to maximize error detection.' The logical asymmetry of falsification — that universal statements are falsifiable but not verifiable — establishes only that falsification is possible and verification is not. By itself it yields no comparative ranking among surviving theories and no reason to prefer the better-corroborated one, because every non-yet-falsified theory equally satisfies the asymmetry. To get from 'all surviving theories are falsifiable' to 'prefer the one with the highest degree of corroboration,' the target must import valuations about severity, informativeness, and error-maximization that are not contained in or entailed by the bare logical asymmetry. Thus the word 'solely' in the claim is false: the defense rests on extra-logical, substantive methodological premises. This is not merely imprecision; it is load-bearing, because the claim's plausibility as a defense 'on Popper's own terms' depends on the preference following from the logical asymmetry alone — if extra premises are required, the target has not shown they are available without smuggling in exactly the non-deductive warrant Popper sought to avoid.
